h1: Teaching a friend to taste whisky
title: Teaching a Friend to Taste Whisky | Craft Beer School
desc: How to teach a friend to taste whisky: the setup, a three whisky flight, the words to use and how to keep the evening responsible and fun.
teaser: Most people are taught to swallow whisky fast. Here is how to show a friend how to taste it instead.
standfirst: Teaching someone else to taste whisky is the quickest way to sharpen your own palate. A short flight, a few rules and a lot of water do most of the work.
sections: Start with what they already know

Most newcomers arrive with one of two ideas: whisky is harsh and must be drowned in cola, or whisky is a test of toughness to be swallowed in one go. Neither leaves room for tasting.

Begin with flavours your friend already knows. Ask what they like in food and drinks: coffee, chocolate, fruit, smoke, spice. Those words are the bridge. If they can tell masala chai from filter coffee by smell, they can learn to taste whisky. The skill is the same, just pointed at a different glass.

A good setup takes ten minutes and makes the evening work.

  • Three whiskies that are clearly different. A light, fruity one, a richer sherry cask or bourbon and a lightly peated one.
  • Matching glasses, ideally tulip shaped, so the glass is not the variable.
  • Pours of about 15 ml each. That is a tasting, not a round of drinks.
  • A jug of water, a small dropper or teaspoon and plain crackers or bread.
  • An empty cup for spitting or pouring away, plus soft drinks for anyone who is not drinking.

Agree before you start that nobody drives afterwards.

Keep the method simple so your friend can repeat it alone.

  1. Look. Note the colour, but explain that colour can come from caramel and is not a reliable guide to age.
  2. Nose. Hold the glass below the chin first, then bring it slowly closer with the mouth slightly open. Short, gentle sniffs, never a deep inhale.
  3. Taste. A small sip, held on the tongue for a few seconds before swallowing or spitting.
  4. Finish. Breathe out through the nose and notice what lingers and for how long.

Our guide to how whisky is made helps answer the inevitable question of where those flavours come from.

The worst thing you can do is tell a friend what they should smell. They will either find it to please you or feel stupid when they do not. Ask open questions instead. Is it sweet or dry? Fruity or grainy? Does it remind you of anything from a kitchen?

Offer a short word list if they are stuck: vanilla, honey, apple, raisin, nuts, pepper, smoke, toffee, citrus. Let them pick. If they say something unexpected, such as green mango or Parle G, take it seriously. Personal references are often the most accurate descriptions a taster has.
Use water as the second lesson

Once the three whiskies have been tasted neat, add a few drops of water to each and taste again. This is often the moment newcomers start to enjoy whisky. Water lowers the alcohol burn and opens up aroma, so flavours that were hidden come forward.

Explain that adding water is not cheating. Many professional blenders nose samples reduced to around 20% ABV precisely because full strength numbs the nose. Our guide to malt, grain and blended whisky is a good follow up for a friend who wants to know why the three glasses tasted so different.

Three 15 ml pours add up to 45 ml of whisky, roughly a large single measure in total. That is plenty. A tasting that runs to six or seven whiskies turns into drinking. The palate stops learning after the first few anyway.

Eat before and during. Drink a glass of water for every whisky. If your friend does not want to finish a pour, encourage them to pour it away. Spitting is normal practice for professional tasters, not a sign of weakness. Nobody gets behind the wheel.

A few habits spoil a first tasting more than any choice of whisky:

  • Starting with the smokiest bottle. Heavy peat first can put a newcomer off for years. Save it for last.
  • Talking too much. Let your friend nose quietly for a minute before you say anything.
  • Correcting their notes. There is no wrong answer at this stage, only a vague one. Ask what it reminds them of instead.
  • Pouring big measures. Large pours turn a lesson into a session. Keep them small.

Teaching also tests your own palate. If your friend finds something you missed, nose the glass again. Beginners often notice what experienced drinkers have stopped looking for.
Where to go after the first evening

A first tasting gives your friend a method and a handful of words. Building a reliable palate takes structured practice: tasting with reference standards, learning to spot faults, calibrating against other tasters and keeping notes over weeks. That is hard to organise between friends. It is exactly what a sensory course is built for.

Before the next session, ask your friend to write three words for one whisky at home and bring them along. Compare notes before you pour anything.
faqs: How many whiskies should a first tasting include?
Three is ideal. It is enough to show contrast without tiring the palate or turning the evening into a drinking session.
How much whisky should I pour for a tasting?
About 15 ml per whisky. Small pours keep the focus on tasting and keep the total alcohol modest.
Should beginners add water to whisky?
Yes, after tasting it neat once. A few drops of water often makes whisky easier and more interesting for newcomers.
Is it rude to spit whisky at a tasting?
No. Spitting is standard practice among professional tasters and is a sensible way to taste several whiskies.
